explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says, “But Jonathan did not tell his father.” (1 Samuel 14:1) Jonathan is Saul's son, and Saul is the king of Israel. No text, no note, no group chat, just a young man and his armor-bearer heading out.
That's right, friend. “But Jonathan did not tell his father.” (1 Samuel 14:1) Jonathan, Saul's son, takes his armor-bearer and goes. Saul is Israel's king, and he's sitting at home with no idea.
Six hundred is right. The troops with Saul at Migron number about six hundred men. That's a small crowd to be standing under one pomegranate tree. I've seen bigger crowds at a half-price cookie sale.

That number is too big for this spot. The text says the troops with Saul at Migron numbered about six hundred men. Saul is the king of Israel, and this is the group sitting with him under the pomegranate tree.
Ten thousand would fill a whole stadium, friend. The text puts the troops with Saul at about six hundred men. That's the crowd around him at Migron, on the outskirts of Gibeah.
Yes, friend. “But the troops did not know that Jonathan had left.” (1 Samuel 14:3) Nobody sees him go. Ahijah the priest is there, and so are about six hundred men, and not one of them knows.

The text says it the other way. “But the troops did not know that Jonathan had left.” (1 Samuel 14:3) He slipped away, and the camp kept right on sitting there. Six hundred men, and not one of them spotted it.
Cliffs it is. The text says there were cliffs on both sides of the pass Jonathan intended to cross. That's not a nice flat walk to the outpost. Whatever happens next, it starts with a climb.
No rivers here, friend. The text says there were cliffs on both sides of the pass. Jonathan has rock walls to deal with, not water.
No towers in this stretch. The text says cliffs stood on both sides of the pass, one named Bozez and the other Seneh. Nobody built them. They were just sitting there, being big.

explanations.answer: Nothing can stop Him from saving by many or by few
explanations.explanation: That's Jonathan's whole case. He says, “Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” Two men against an outpost is a small number. He doesn't count heads, because he's looking at who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: He only saves when the army is big enough
explanations.explanation: Jonathan says the opposite. “Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” He's walking toward an outpost with exactly one other man. If he believed the army had to be big, he'd have stayed under that pomegranate tree.

explanations.answer: He will fight for them once Saul arrives
explanations.explanation: Saul isn't even part of this plan, friend. Jonathan didn't tell his father he was leaving (1 Samuel 14:1). What Jonathan does say is, “Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.”

explanations.answer: Go ahead and I am with you
explanations.explanation: That's it. His armor-bearer says, “Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul.” He isn't looking for an exit. I think that's the kind of friend you want when your plan sounds bold.

explanations.answer: Go back and ask your father first
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say that at all. Jonathan hadn't told his father (1 Samuel 14:1), and the armor-bearer answers, “Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul.” No stalling, no extra questions.

explanations.answer: Wait here until more men come
explanations.explanation: He's not stalling, friend. The armor-bearer says, “Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul.” He doesn't ask for more men, and he doesn't ask for more time. He just picks up his feet and goes.

Right. Jonathan says, “then we will stay where we are and will not go up to them.” If the Philistines say wait, the two of them wait. The plan is simple. What the outpost says decides what Jonathan does.
Not on that answer. Jonathan says, “If they say, ‘Wait until we come to you,’ then we will stay where we are and will not go up to them.” The climbing only happens on the other answer.
No retreat in this plan, friend. Jonathan says, “then we will stay where we are and will not go up to them.” They hold their ground right there. Saul's camp never comes up.

explanations.answer: Their sign the LORD has handed them over
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jonathan says, “But if they say, ‘Come on up,’ then we will go up, because this will be our sign that the LORD has delivered them into our hands.” The invitation from the outpost is the sign. It's an odd thing to wait on, but that's the plan.

explanations.answer: Their sign to go back and get Saul
explanations.explanation: That's not in the plan. Jonathan says “Come on up” will be, “our sign that the LORD has delivered them into our hands.” Saul never comes up in what Jonathan says.

explanations.answer: Their sign that the outpost is a trap
explanations.explanation: Jonathan reads it the other way. He says, “this will be our sign that the LORD has delivered them into our hands.” If the Philistines say “Come on up,” the two of them go up.

explanations.answer: Come on up and we will teach you a lesson
explanations.explanation: That's the sign Jonathan was waiting for. The men of the outpost call out, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” They think it's a threat. Jonathan says, “Follow me… for the LORD has delivered them into the hand of Israel.”

explanations.answer: Wait there until we come down to you
explanations.explanation: That was the other option, and it isn't what they say. The men of the outpost call out, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” So the two men get their answer, and it means go.

explanations.answer: Turn around and go back to your homes
explanations.explanation: Nobody sends them home, friend. The men of the outpost call out, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” They're inviting Jonathan up, and it sounds like a threat to them.

That's what the text says. “And the Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and finished them off.” (1 Samuel 14:13) Two men climbed up the cliff on their hands and feet. The outpost that promised a lesson didn't get the way it planned.
That would've been the scary version. The text says, “the Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and finished them off.” Nobody closes in on him. They go down.
No captives here, friend. The text says, “the Philistines fell before Jonathan.” His armor-bearer follows behind him and finishes them off.

Twenty is right. In that first assault, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men in about half an acre of land. It's a small patch of ground for a big moment. Two men started that day's story, and it's only getting bigger.
That's too high, friend. The text says about twenty men fell in that first assault. It also says it all happened in about half an acre of land.

Two hundred is way more than the text gives. In that first assault, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men. That's about twenty, in about half an acre. The rest of the story comes from what happens next.
True. The text says, “Indeed, the earth quaked, and panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15) The ground shakes along with the Philistines. That's a lot of trembling in one place.
The text says the ground shakes too. “Indeed, the earth quaked, and panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15) The Philistines are trembling, and so is the earth under them.
Right. The text says, “panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15) Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men, and then the whole Philistine camp shook. That part came from God.

Jonathan did strike down about twenty men, but that's not where the panic comes from. The text says, “panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15) Two men couldn't shake a whole camp, a field and every outpost on their own.
Saul isn't even there yet, friend. He's still back with his troops, and he's about to find out Jonathan is gone. The text says, “panic spread from God.” (1 Samuel 14:15)

explanations.answer: Call the roll and see who has left
explanations.explanation: That's what Saul says. “Call the roll and see who has left us.” His watchmen have seen the Philistine troops melting away, so he wants a head count. The roll shows Jonathan and his armor-bearer are not there.

explanations.answer: Sound the horn and gather all Israel
explanations.explanation: That's not his first move. Saul says to the troops with him, “Call the roll and see who has left us.” He starts with a head count. I think he wants to know who's missing before he does anything else.

explanations.answer: Go and spy on the Philistine camp
explanations.explanation: No spies are sent. Saul tells the troops with him, “Call the roll and see who has left us.” That's how he finds out Jonathan and his armor-bearer are gone.

Yes. While Saul is talking to the priest, “the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase.” Things are getting louder over there while Saul is still talking. So Saul tells the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”

explanations.answer: The Philistines calm down and regroup
explanations.explanation: It goes the other direction, friend. The text says, “the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase.” The Philistines aren't settling down. That's why Saul stops talking to the priest.

explanations.answer: The Philistines send men toward Gibeah
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says, “the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase.” The Philistines are busy with their own camp.

That's what they find. Saul and all his troops march to the battle, “and they found the Philistines in total confusion.” Everyone over there is mixed up and swinging at the wrong people. It's like a kitchen where every timer goes off at once.

explanations.answer: A Philistine camp left completely empty
explanations.explanation: The camp isn't empty. The text says Saul's troops “found the Philistines in total confusion.” There are plenty of Philistines, and they can't tell who is who.

explanations.answer: Philistines lined up and ready to fight
explanations.explanation: Nobody's lined up over there. The text says Saul's troops “found the Philistines in total confusion.” Each man is swinging his sword at his neighbor.

The text says they switch sides. “And the Hebrews who had previously gone up into the surrounding camps to join the Philistines now went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.” (1 Samuel 14:21) They don't stay put. They go over to the Israelites.

Right, friend. The Hebrews who had gone up to join the Philistines “now went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.” (1 Samuel 14:21) They switch sides, and the Israelite side keeps growing.

explanations.answer: Join the battle and chase them
explanations.explanation: Yes. The Israelites hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard the Philistines were fleeing, “they also joined the battle in close pursuit.” (1 Samuel 14:22) They come out of hiding to chase them. The hills empty out fast.

explanations.answer: Stay hidden up in the hills
explanations.explanation: They come out of the hills. When they hear the Philistines are fleeing, “they also joined the battle in close pursuit.” (1 Samuel 14:22) The hiding is over.
No waiting in the stands, friend. The text says they “also joined the battle in close pursuit.” (1 Samuel 14:22) They hear the Philistines are fleeing, and they run right after them.

That's what the text says. “So the LORD saved Israel that day.” (1 Samuel 14:23) Two men climbed a cliff, and the panic spread from God. It's the same thing Jonathan said at the start, that nothing can hinder the LORD from saving.
The text names someone else. “So the LORD saved Israel that day.” (1 Samuel 14:23) Saul's army was only about six hundred men, and the first strike came from two.
The text gives the credit somewhere else. “So the LORD saved Israel that day.” (1 Samuel 14:23) Saul is the king, and he spent the start of this story back at the pomegranate tree.
